en: Praśnopaniṣad: Oṃ. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, may we praise [you] and enjoy that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his uninjured wheel-rims grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace! Peace! Peace!
The first question:
this Brāhmaṇa is commenced as a detailed restatement of the meaning expressed in the mantra;
the narrative consisting of the questions and answers of the sages, however, is for the purpose of praising the knowledge.

Thus, this [knowledge] is to be received from teachers who are like omniscient ones—such as Pippalāda and others—who have been endowed with practices such as living in celibacy for a year; it is not to be spoken by just anyone. In this way, he praises the knowledge. Furthermore, because the means such as celibacy are indicated, their necessity as duties follows. Om.
Sukeśa Bhāradvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya, Kausalya Āśvalāyana,
Bhārgava Vaidarbhi, and Kabandhī Kātyāyana— these, devoted to Brahman, grounded in Brahman, seeking the Supreme Brahman, [approached Pippalāda].
"He will indeed tell us all that," they said, and with fuel in their hands, they approached the venerable Pippalāda.
Sukeśa by name,
Bhāradvāja as the offspring of Bharadvāja,
Śaibya as the offspring of Śibi, and Satyakāma by name.
Sauryāyaṇī: Sūrya is [the name of] a person; his offspring is Saurya; his offspring is Sauryāyaṇi—this form "Sauryāyaṇī" is Vedic (chāndasa).
Gārgya is the offspring of the Garga lineage. Bhārgava is the descendant of Bhṛgu. Vaidarbhi means one who is born in Vidarbha. Kabandhī is [his] name.
*Katyasyāpasyaṃ Kātyāyanaḥ*: he whose paternal great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) is still living;
[the suffix] *yuvan* is applied [here].

They were devoted to Brahman; having reached the Supreme Brahman as their ultimate goal and being steadfast in its practice, they were established in Brahman. Seeking the Supreme Brahman—asking "What is that which is to be eternally known?"—and thinking, "We shall strive according to our desire for the sake of attaining that," they conducted this search. For the purpose of attaining it, thinking, "This one indeed will tell us all that," they approached a teacher. How so? With fuel in their hands—that is, with fuel-sticks held in their hands—they approached and waited upon the venerable Pippalāda, their teacher.
The seer said to them:
"Dwell for another year with austerity, celibacy, and faith."
"Ask questions as you wish;
if we understand them, we shall explain everything to you. (Praśna Upaniṣad 1.2)

When they had approached him in this manner, that sage spoke to them once again: "Even though you have previously practiced austerity through the restraint of the senses, nevertheless, you shall dwell here for a period of one year, practicing celibacy with faith and a mind of conviction, remaining fully devoted to the service of the teacher."
Therefore, according to your desire—without overstepping whatever each individual desires—and according to your inclination, ask questions concerning whatever subject you wish to know.

If we should not understand that which is asked by you—the word "if" (*yadi*) is used for the purpose of demonstrating humility and does not imply ignorance or doubt, as is evident from the resolution of the question—"we shall indeed explain everything that has been asked by you. (2)
Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana approached and asked:
"Venerable sir, from what indeed are these creatures born?"
Then, after a year had passed, Kabandhī Kātyāyana approached and, having drawn near, asked:
"O Venerable One, from where, indeed, are these creatures—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—born?
This question is intended to elicit an explanation of the result and the destination that arise from the combined practice of the lower knowledge and ritual action. //3//
To him he said:
"Prajāpati, indeed, was desirous of offspring."
He performed austerity.
Having performed austerity, he brought forth a pair: Rayi (Wealth) and Prāṇa (Life-breath), thinking, "These two shall produce offspring for me in many ways. (PrU 1.4)
To him who had thus questioned, he spoke this in order to refute that [objection]:

Prajāpati, desiring offspring— that is, wishing to emit offspring from himself— being the Self of all, possessing the realization "I shall create the entire world," acting according to what has been said, and permeated by that state of being, emerges at the beginning of the kalpa as Hiraṇyagarbha for the sake of those beings who are to be created.

The Lord of all beings, both stationary and moving, reflected upon— that is, performed penance for— the knowledge cultivated through previous births, which has as its object the meaning revealed by the Vedas (*śruti*). Thus, having performed such penance and having reflected upon the Vedic knowledge, he produced a pair (*mithuna*), that is, a couple, which serves as the means for creation.

Thinking, "May these two, Agni and Soma— wealth (rayi), Soma, food (anna), and breath (praṇa), with Agni as the eater— having become the eaters of food, create for me offspring in many ways, in manifold ways," he fashioned the sun and the moon according to the sequence of the production of the cosmic egg.
The sun, indeed, is breath; the moon is wealth. All this that is both formed and formless is indeed wealth.
Therefore, form alone is wealth.
In this context, the sun is indeed the breath, the eater; Agni is the food;
and the moon is wealth, for it is wealth.
Thus, Soma is indeed food; this is that which is both the eater and the food. Prajāpati, however, is the single couple.
The distinction is made on the basis of what is subordinate and what is primary.
How so? All this is indeed wealth (*rayi*) or food (*anna*).
What is that? Whatever is formed (*mūrta*), whether gross or unformed (*amūrta*), whether subtle or not—both the formed and the unformed, in their nature as food, are simply wealth.

Therefore, that which is other than the formless and so forth, being distinguished from them, is the formal; "form" (mūrti) is indeed "wealth" (rayi), because it is being consumed by the formless. //5//
Likewise, although formless, it is also that which consists of breath and all that is to be eaten.
How so?—

Now, as the sun rises, in that it enters the eastern quarter, it places the eastern vital breaths within its rays;
in that it illuminates the south, the west, the north, the nadir, the zenith, the intermediate directions, and everything—all that, it places all the vital breaths within its rays.
Now, as the sun rises, ascending and coming within the range of vision of living beings, it enters—that is, pervades—the eastern direction with its own light.
Because it is pervasive within those things that possess pervasion in the form of the illumination of its own self, it brings living beings together, it causes them to settle;
the meaning is that it makes them one with itself.

In the same way, that which enters the south, the west, the north, below, above, and that which enters the intermediate directions, the corner directions, the sub-directions, and whatever else it illumines— by means of that pervasion of its own light, it withdraws all the vital breaths situated in every direction into its rays. //6//

This very Vaiśvānara, the universal-formed breath, rises as fire. Regarding this, a verse was sung by Dakṣa: START PrUp 1.8 "The face of truth has risen in the east; the eye of the world shines in the middle. The arms of the immortal are on both sides; the feet of the earth are established in the north. PrUp_1.8 // PrUp_1.9 "Truth is the head, the eye is the sun, the two arms are the wind, the feet are the earth; the navel is the ether, the heart is the moon, and from the mouth comes fire—thus did they conceive of the all-pervading one. His greatness is indeed as great as the greatness of Vaiśvānara. As far as the extent of fire, so far is the extent of his world, and he wins as much as that. This very one is the Eater, the Prāṇa Vaiśvānara, the Self of all, whose form is the universe; and because he is the self of all, both Prāṇa and Agni are that same Eater who rises up—emerges every day, making all the quarters his own.
This very reality has also been declared by a Ṛk verse, a mantra: //7//

The omniform, golden-hued Jātavedas, the ultimate resort, the single light that blazes— this Sun, the life-breath of all creatures, rises with a thousand rays, manifesting itself in a hundred ways. (PrUp 1.8)

The wise, the knowers of Brahman, have realized their own Self as the Sun— the one of universal form, possessing all forms, the golden-hued, the radiant, the knower of all that is born, the source of manifested wisdom, the ultimate refuge, the abode of all vital breaths, the singular light that has become the eye of all living beings, the non-dual, burning and performing the act of heating.
Who is this whom they have come to know?

This is the sun, the breath (*prāṇa*) of living beings, which rises with a thousand rays, many rays, existing in a hundred ways and manifold ways according to the different classes of creatures. //8//

That moon which is the formed [element] is food, and the formless is the vital breath, the eater; that sun is this single couple. How will they produce all creatures? It is said: Prajāpati is indeed the year.
Its paths are the southern and the northern.
Those who indeed worship that as "the performance of sacrifice and pious works" (iṣṭāpūrta) win the world of the moon alone;
they return again.
Therefore, these seers, desiring offspring, proceed by the southern path;
for that which is the path of the fathers is indeed wealth.
That very thing is Time; indeed, Prajāpati is the year, because the year is brought about by him.

Because the year is brought about by the moon and the sun—the year being a collection of lunar days, days and nights, and so forth—it is said to consist of nothing other than that, having the nature of the union of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the ray (rayi).

How is that so? Of that Prajāpati, the year, there are two paths (ayana), the southern and the northern; for these two well-known paths, characterized by six months each, are those by which the Sun travels, bestowing worlds upon those who perform mere ritual acts and those who possess actions conjoined with knowledge.
How so? Regarding the phrase "those Brahmins and others who indeed worship that" (*ye ha vai tad upāsate*), the second word *tat* is an adverbial modifier of the action;

they worship only what has been performed—namely, "sacrifices and works of public utility" (*iṣṭāpūrte*) and so forth—not what is unperformed or eternal. And they [attain] the lunar world (*cāndramasam*), which exists in the moon (*candramasi bhavam*), belonging to the moon (*prājāpatyam*).
For it has been stated: "Having reached their end right there, they return again; they enter this world or one even lower" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.10).
This is because, by means of the very acts of sacrifice and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), they bring about Prajāpati—who consists of food—as their fruit, namely the moon.

The seers (*ṛṣis*), who behold heaven, being desirous of offspring and seeking progeny, are householders; therefore, they proceed toward the south, which is their own making—the moon characterized by the southern course. This indeed is "wealth" (*rayi*), that is, food (*anna*), which is characterized by the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*). //9//
Then, having sought the Self by means of austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, they conquer the sun.
This indeed is the abode of the vital breaths, this is the immortal, this is the ultimate goal.
"From this they do not return again"—this is cessation. Regarding that, there is this verse: PrUp 1.10.
Then, by the northern course, they conquer the Sun—Prajāpati’s portion, the vital breath, the consumer. By what means?

Through austerity, the conquest of the senses, and especially through celibacy, faith, and knowledge. Having sought out the Self—the vital breath, the Sun—which is the self of Prajāpati and the essence of all that moves and stands, and having realized "I am He," they conquer and attain the Sun.
This indeed is the abode, the common abode and support for all living beings; it is immortal and imperishable.
It is fearless, and for that very reason devoid of fear, unlike the moon which possesses the fear of waning and waxing.
This is the supreme goal, the ultimate resort for those possessed of knowledge and those engaged in ritual action alike.
"From this they do not return again, as others who are mere performers of ritual acts do.
Since this is the cessation for the ignorant—
those ignorant ones who have ceased [their movement] with respect to the sun and so forth do not reach the year, nor the sun, nor the self, nor the vital breath.
For that year is the cessation of time for those who do not know;
with regard to this matter, there is this verse as a mantra.
They say that the Father has five feet and twelve forms, and that he dwells in the watery realm in the further half of heaven.
But others say that he, the far-seeing one, is fixed upon a seven-wheeled, six-spoked chariot. // PrUp 1.11 //

It has five feet; the five seasons are like its feet. That Āditya, whose self is the year, revolves by means of those feet, which are the seasons. This conceptualization is made by treating Hemanta and Śiśira as one.
He is the "Father" (Pitṛ) because he is the progenitor of all.

They— the knowers of time— call him "twelve-formed," for his forms or limbs are the twelve months, or rather, his formation consists of the arrangement of these twelve months; they call him "full of *purīṣa*," meaning full of water, situated above the sky, in the world of heaven— in the third heaven, so to speak.

Then others, who understand time, call that very same [Self] the "Three-eyed," the "Subtle," and the "All-knowing. They say that this entire world is fixed within the Self of Time— which consists of seven wheels and takes the form of seven horses, which is constantly in motion, and which has six spokes corresponding to the six seasons—
just as spokes are set upon the hub of a chariot wheel.

Whether it has five feet and twelve forms, or seven wheels and six spokes—in every way, the year itself, as the temporal self and Prajāpati, characterized by the moon and the sun, is the cause of the world. //11//
START PrUp 1.12:
He in whom this entire universe is supported is indeed Prajāpati, known as the Year; he is fully completed within his own constituent part, the month.
For the month is indeed Prajāpati.
His wealth is indeed the dark fortnight, and his life-breath is the bright fortnight.
Therefore, these seers perform sacrifices during the bright fortnight, while others do so during the other.
The month is indeed Prajāpati, possessing the characteristics already described and consisting of a pair.
Of that Prajāpati who is the month, one part is the dark fortnight, which is wealth, food, and the moon;
the other part is the bright fortnight, which is wealth, food, and the moon.

The other portion is the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the sun, and the eater, Agni. Because they see the entire self of the bright fortnight as the vital breath, these seers (*ṛṣi*)—who perceive the vital breath—do not see the dark fortnight. But others, because they do not perceive the vital breath, see only the dark self, which is characterized by non-perception.
In the other case, they perform [the rite] only during the dark fortnight, even though they may also perform it during the bright fortnight.
The day and night, indeed, are Prajāpati. Of him,
the day is breath and the night is wealth.
Those who unite in sexual pleasure during the day indeed spill their vital breath;
when they unite in sexual pleasure at night, that is truly the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
That Prajāpati, consisting of a month, is also completed within his own parts, day and night;
for day and night are indeed Prajāpati, as before. Of that [month] as well, the day is the breath, the eater, and fire; the night is indeed wealth, as before.

It is these fools who, by day during the daytime, unite with a woman—the cause of sexual pleasure—and engage in copulation; they thus spill forth, emit, or dry up their own life-force (prāṇa) and soul (ātman), severing it from themselves and casting it away.
Since this is so, the prohibition "therefore that must not be done" follows as a relevant corollary.

Since it is praised that "whatever union occurs at night during the fertile period is indeed celibacy," this is also an incidental injunction that one should approach one's wife during the fertile period.
Now, however, the subject at hand is stated: that Prajāpati, consisting of day and night, is established in the form of food such as rice and barley. (13)
Thus, having transformed in this sequence—
that food is indeed Prajāpati; from that, indeed, comes semen.
Therefore, these creatures are born. // PrUp 1.14 //
Food, indeed, is Prajāpati.
How so? From that, indeed, comes semen—the seed of man, the cause of progeny—from which, when infused into a woman, these creatures characterized as humans and so forth are born.
This answers the question asked: "From what, indeed, are creatures born?"

Thus, it has been determined that these creatures are born through the sequence beginning with the union of the moon and the sun, ending with day and night, by means of the extraction of food, blood, and semen. //14//
Now, those who indeed observe that vow of Prajāpati produce a pair.
This world of Brahman belongs only to those for whom austerity and celibacy are the rule,
and in whom truth is firmly established.

This being so, those householders—who—*ha vai* being particles used for well-known recollection—perform that vow of Prajāpati, the *prajāpativrata*, namely approaching their wife during her season (*ṛtu*)—for them this is the visible fruit:
what is it? They procreate a pair, a son and a daughter.

And the unseen fruit belongs to those who perform sacrifices (iṣṭa), public works (pūrta), and acts of charity (datta); it is for them alone that this lunar world of Brahman exists, which is characterized as the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa).

This applies to those whose austerity consists of the vows of a Snātaka and the like, whose celibacy (brahmacarya) is observed, and in whom truth—defined as the avoidance of falsehood—is firmly established and persists at all times without deviation. //15//

But that which is characterized by the sun—the state of the self as *prāṇa* during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*)—is free from passion (*viraja*), pure, and unlike the world of the moon or the world of Brahmā, which is subject to passion, growth, decay, and so forth. For whom is this? It is said:
"This passionless world of Brahman belongs to those in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood, and no deceit. (PrU 1.16)

Just as deceit (*jihmā*), crookedness, and insincerity are inevitable for householders because they must engage in various conflicting worldly transactions, so too there is no such deceit among them; and just as falsehood is unavoidable for householders on account of play, jesting, and the like, so too there is none among them; likewise, the guile characteristic of householders does not exist among them.
*Māyā* is that which, having manifested itself externally in one way, performs its effect in quite another way; it is of the nature of deceitful conduct.

In those qualified persons—namely the student (*brahmacārin*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*)—such defects as *māyā* and the like do not exist because of the absence of their causes. Consequently, for them, that world of Brahman is free from passion (*virajaḥ*) in accordance with their means.
This is the destination for those who possess action conjoined with knowledge.
However, the previously mentioned world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), characterized as the moon, belongs solely to those who perform ritual actions. //16//
Thus ends the first question.
The second question: It has been stated that Prāṇa is the eater and Prajāpati.
To establish that his status as Prajāpati and his nature as the Eater must be understood in reference to this very body, the following question is introduced:
Then Bhārgava Vaidarbhi questioned him.
"Blessed One, how many gods sustain the creatures?
Which among them illuminate this?
And who, moreover, is the most excellent of them? (PrU 2.1)
Immediately after that, it is said, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi questioned him:
"O Blessed One, how many gods indeed specifically sustain—that is, uphold—the creation characterized by the body?
Which among them manifest this illumination, which is the proclamation of their own majesty, through the division of the organs of perception and the organs of action?"
Furthermore, which among these—characterized as effects and instruments—is the most excellent and the primary? //1//
To him he said:
"Verily, this god is space; it is wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, sight, and hearing."
Having revealed themselves, they said:
"It is we who, having taken hold of this arrow, support it. (PrUp 2.2)

To him who had thus questioned, he said: "Verily, this god is space; [and] wind, fire, water, and earth—these five great elements that initiate the body; as well as speech, mind, sight, hearing, and so forth, including the organs of action and the organs of perception.
These gods, characterized by their effects and characterized by their instruments, proclaiming their own greatness, speak while contending for preeminence, saying, 'I am the best!'"
How do they say it?
"We, having taken hold of this body—a collection of causes and effects—just as pillars and other supports do for a palace, maintain it without letting it fall apart; we hold it clearly. [2]
Then the preeminent Prāṇa said to them:
"Do not fall into delusion."
"It is I myself who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this arrow.
They were not inclined to believe him.
To those who were thus possessed of such conceit, the preeminent and principal Prāṇa spoke, saying:

"Do not fall into this delusion; do not, through lack of discrimination, harbor such pride. For it is I alone who, having divided myself fivefold into the various functions of prāṇa and so forth, support and sustain this body by holding it firm. Thus he spoke.
And placing their trust in him, they became full of confidence, wondering, "How can this be so? //3//
Starting from *PrUp* 2.4:
On account of his conceit, he seems to ascend upward.
When he ascends, then all the others indeed ascend after him.
And as he stands, they all stand;
just as when the king of the bees flies up, they all fly up together,
and when he stands still, they all stand still.
In the same way, speech, mind, sight, and hearing—
being delighted, they praise the vital breath.

And that vital breath (prāṇa), perceiving their lack of faith, as if rising up out of pride, departed from him as it were; when it departed, full of wrath and indifferent, he makes what occurred visible by means of an illustration:
when that one had departed, immediately thereafter all the other vital breaths, beginning with the eye, departed and went forth together.
And when that vital breath (prāṇa) was settling down, it became silent; as it departed, all indeed settled down and remained silent.

In this regard, it is just as in the world when the bees—the honey-makers—follow their own king, the king of the honey-makers, as he departs, and when he settles down, they all settle down and take their stand.
Just as in this illustration, so too speech, mind, sight, hearing, and the others—having abandoned their lack of faith and understood the greatness of Prāṇa, they praise Prāṇa with joy. //4//
How so?
This one is Agni who burns; this one is Sūrya; this one is Parjanya Maghavan; this one is Vāyu.
This earth is wealth; it is the god, that which exists and that which is immortal.
This vital breath (prāṇa), being fire, heats and blazes;
likewise, being the sun, it shines;
and likewise, being the rain-cloud, it rains.
Furthermore, as Maghavan Indra, he protects the subjects from of old and seeks to slay the Asuras and Rakshasas;
this is Vayu, distinguished by its various modes such as Āvaha and Pravaha.

Moreover, this is the earth, wealth, the god, the foundation of the entire world—both that which is formed and that which is formless, both the mortal and the immortal; indeed, it is the cause of the stability of the gods. What more need be said? //5//
As the spokes are fixed in the nave of a wheel, so everything is established in the vital breath (prāṇa):
the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the sacrifice, the ruling power, and the spiritual authority.
Just as the spokes are fixed in the nave of a wheel, so at the time of sustenance, everything from faith (śraddhā) down to name (nāman) is established in the vital breath (prāṇa) alone.

Likewise, the threefold mantras—the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants—as well as the sacrifice accomplished by them, the Kṣatra which protects all, and the Brāhmaṇa who is authorized to perform the rites of sacrifice and so forth—all this is indeed this Prāṇa. 6.
Moreover:
"O Prajāpati, you move within the womb; you alone are born again."
To you, O Prāṇa, these creatures bring tribute, you who are established through the vital breaths.
He who is Prajāpati is indeed you yourself as you move within the womb; being the counterpart of both father and mother, you are born again.
Precisely because of your status as Prajāpati, your nature as mother and father was already established even prior to this.
The meaning is that Prāṇa alone is the self of all, possessing the forms of all bodies and their inhabitants, as well as of the mind.
O Prāṇa, these creatures—humans and others—are offering tribute for your sake through the doors of the eyes and other senses.
Since you, together with the vital breaths such as the eyes and so forth, are established in all bodies, it is fitting that they offer tribute to you.
For since you are the enjoyer, everything else belongs to you as the object of enjoyment. //7//
Moreover:
You are the foremost bearer of offerings for the gods; you are the first funeral oblation for the ancestors.
You are the true conduct of the sages, the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases.
Among the gods, beginning with Indra, you are the most excellent bearer (*vahnitama*), the best deliverer of the oblations.
In the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha for the ancestors, the *svadhā* food which is offered to the ancestors becomes primary when considered in relation to the gods;

the meaning is that you alone are the deliverer of even that [food] to the ancestors. Furthermore, [you are the deliverer] of the seers (*ṛṣi*), of the vital breaths such as sight and so forth, of the Aṅgirases—those who have become Aṅgirases—and of the Atharvans, for it is said of them: "The Atharvan is indeed the vital breath."
You alone are the conduct, the activity, the truth, and the non-erroneous nature characterized by the assistance of sustaining the body and so forth. //8//
"O Prāṇa, by your splendor you are Indra; you are Rudra when withdrawing the world. And in its maintenance, you are the protector, the guardian, and the one who guards it on all sides."
You alone, in your gentle form, move eternally through the intermediate space by means of rising and setting; you alone are the Sun and the lord of all luminaries.
O Prāṇa, you are Indra, the Supreme Lord; by your splendor and heroic power, you are Rudra, the destroyer of the world.
And in the maintenance of the world, you alone are the protector, the preserver, and the guardian on all sides with your gentle form.
You move incessantly in the intermediate space through rising and setting; you are indeed the Sun and the lord of all luminaries. //9//
But when you rain down, O Prāṇa, these creatures of yours exist in a state of bliss, thinking, "Food will come according to our desire."
When you become Parjanya (the rain-cloud) and pour down rain, then these creatures obtain food and "prāṇanti"—that is, they perform the activity of breathing.

Alternatively, these creatures of yours, who have become one with your own self and are nourished by your food, remain as if they have attained bliss and happiness merely at the sight of your pouring down rain; their intention is that food will be available according to their desire. //10//
Moreover:
"O Prāṇa, you are the Vrātya, the sole seer, the eater of all, and the lord of beings."
We are the givers of the first [oblation]; you, O Mātariśvan, are our father.
The intention is that, because you were born first and there was no other purifier [before you], you are unrefined; yet as a *vrātya*, you are pure by your very nature.
O sole consumer of vital breath (*prāṇaikarṣi*), you are the fire known among the followers of the Atharvaveda by the name Ekarṣi, the eater of all oblations.
You alone are the lord (*pati*) of the entire existing world, the lord of what is real (*satpati*).
The husband is virtuous, a true lord (*satpati*).
We, moreover, are the givers of the first oblation (*havis*) to be consumed by you.
O Mātariśvan, you are our father; O Mātariśvan, [belonging] to us!
Or rather, you are Mātariśvan, the wind;
and from this, your status as the father of the entire world is established. //11//
What more need be said?—
That body of yours which is established in speech, that which is in the ear, and that which is in the eye;
And whatever continuity exists in the mind, make that auspicious; do not depart from it.
That body of yours which is established in speech, performing the activity of speaking through the faculty of the speaker;

that which is in the ear, and that which is in the eye; and that body which is pervasive and continuous in the mind through activities such as volition—make that body auspicious and peaceful. Do not depart; do not make it inauspicious by departing.
What need is there for more?
"Everything here, even that which is established in the third heaven, is under the control of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Like a mother protecting her sons, protect us; bestow upon us prosperity and wisdom. (PrUp 2.13)

In this world, everything whatsoever that constitutes the objects of enjoyment is under the control of Prāṇa alone; and even that multitude of enjoyments belonging to the gods and others which is established in the third heaven (tridiva), Prāṇa alone is their ruler and protector.
Therefore, protect and sustain us, as a mother protects her sons.

"For the brahminical and kṣatriya fortunes have you as their cause; therefore, O Śrī, you who are both Fortune and Wisdom, ordain for us those fortunes and that wisdom which has its basis in your own stability—'vidhasva' means 'ordain' (vidhehi).
Thus, having had his greatness revealed through the praise of the vital breaths beginning with speech by virtue of being the Self of all, the Prāṇa is determined to be Prajāpati, the Eater. 13.

Then Kausalya Āśvalāyana questioned him:
"Venerable sir, from where is this vital breath born?
How does it enter into this body?"
Or, having divided itself, how does it abide? By what does it depart? How does it designate the external?
What is meant by "within"? (PrU 3.1)
Then Kausalya Āśvalāyana questioned him:

"Since the vital breath (prāṇa), though its greatness has been realized through the vital functions whose true nature has been determined, may still be subject to destruction due to its composite nature, I ask, O Blessed One: for what reason does this [breath] enter this body? What is the cause for its assumption of a body? This is the meaning.

And having entered the body, how—in what manner—does the Self, having divided itself, establish itself; or by what specific mode of functioning does it depart from this body? And how does it sustain—that is, maintain—the external, consisting of the elements (adhibhūta) and the divine (adhidaivata); and how the internal (adhyātma)? Thus [he asks].
The word "maintains" (dhārayati) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. //1//
Being thus questioned, he said to him: "START PrUp 3.2" [to him] he said.
"You ask questions that go too far;
you are most proficient in the Veda.
Therefore, I shall speak to you. (PrU 3.2)
To him the teacher said:
"Prāṇa alone, because it is so difficult to understand, is worthy of these difficult questions; yet you ask even about its birth and so forth, and thus you ask questions that go beyond the limit.
You are most devoted to Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*), for you are preeminently a knower of Brahman; therefore, being pleased with you, I shall tell you what you have asked—listen. //2//
From the Self this vital breath is born;
as this shadow is upon a person, so is that [breath] extended within this [Self].
By means of mental action, it enters into this body.
This vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be born from the Self, which is the Supreme Person, the Imperishable, and the Truth.
How so? Here is an illustration:
just as in the world, when a person characterized by a head, hands, and so forth serves as the cause, the resulting shadow is produced; in the same way, this [breath] arises within this Brahman.
The principle called *prāṇa*, which is of the nature of unreality and stands in the place of a shadow, is spread out and offered up within the True Person (*puruṣa*).

It is like a shadow in the body, produced by the mental faculty—that is, caused by karma accomplished through the mind’s volitions, desires, and so forth; for he will say later: “By merit, [one attains] merit” (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.7), and so on.
That very same [shadow] is described as: “Attached, together with their karma” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
And from another Vedic text: "It comes" means it arrives in this body. //3//
Just as a sovereign king appoints his officials,
saying, "Rule over these villages, rule over those villages."
In the same way, this vital breath (prāṇa) places the other vital breaths each separately.

Just as in the world a king or a sovereign emperor appoints officials over villages and other districts—how so? saying, "Rule over these villages, rule over those villages"—in the very same way as this illustration, this chief vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) places and appoints the other vital breaths, such as sight and the rest, as well as its own specific parts, each separately in their respective locations. //4//
Therein is the distribution:
the apāna [breath] is in the anus and the generative organ.
The eye and the ear, and the breath through the mouth and nostrils, each establishes itself by itself;
but the *samāna* [breath] is in the middle,
for it carries this offered food equally.
Therefore, these become the seven flames.

In the "anus and genitals" (*pāyūpastha*)— that is, in that which consists of both the anus and the genitals— the *apāna* breath, which is a division of the self, remains and is present there, performing the function of expelling urine, feces, and so forth. Likewise, in the "eyes and ears" (*cakṣuḥśrotra*)— that is, in that which consists of both the eyes and the ears— [the *udāna* breath remains].

And the *prāṇa* (out-breath), emerging from both the mouth and the nose— that is, from the mouth and the nose (*mukhanāsikābhyām*)— establishes itself, being like a sovereign (*samrāṭ*) in its own right; meanwhile, in the middle, at the navel— the station of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—
it is called *samāna* because it carries equally (*samam*) what is eaten and drunk.

For this reason— since it evenly distributes this food that has been eaten, consumed, or drunk and cast into its own presence— the sevenfold rays or flames go forth from the fire of the stomach toward the region of the heart once it has reached there by means of the fuel of what was eaten and drunk; these are the rays located in the head.
The intended meaning is that there is an illumination of objects such as form, characterized by seeing, hearing, and so forth, through the gateway of the vital breath (prāṇa). //5//
For this Self is in the heart;
here there are these one hundred and one channels.
Of each of these there are one hundred;
thus there are seventy-two thousand secondary branch-nerves. Within these the vyāna breath moves.
Thus, within this space of the heart, which is demarcated by a lump of flesh shaped like a lotus, this Self—the subtle body (liṅgātman)—is joined with the [individual] self.
Here, in this heart, there are one hundred and one principal channels in number.
Of these, there are one hundred branches for each of the principal channels.
Furthermore, there are seventy-two thousand, two thousand more, seventy thousand, and seventy-two thousand secondary branch-nerves (*pratiśākhā-nāḍī*).
For each hundred of these branches, there are thousands of primary nerves by that same count.
Within these nerves, the *vyāna* wind moves; it is called *vyāna* because of its pervasive nature (*vyāpanāt*).
Like rays from the sun, the vyāna breath pervades the entire body through the all-pervading channels (nāḍīs) originating from the heart;

it functions specifically in the joints, shoulders, and vital points (marmans), and in the interval between the activities of prāṇa and apāna, it manifests its activity as the performer of powerful actions. //6//
Now,
by means of one [channel], the *udāna* breath, moving upwards, leads [the person] to a virtuous world by virtue of their merit, and to a sinful world by virtue of their sin.
By both together, one attains the world of men.

Now, among those one hundred and one channels, that channel which goes upward and is called *suṣumnā*— through it the *udāna* breath, moving upward and functioning from the soles of the feet to the head, leads by means of meritorious action prescribed by the scriptures to a meritorious world characterized by the abodes of gods and the like; and by means of sinful action, which is the opposite of that, it leads to a sinful state characterized by hell, animal births, and so forth.
It follows that it is by both merit and demerit, which are of equal importance, that one is led to the world of humans. //7//
The sun, indeed, is the external vital breath; for it rises,
sustaining this vital breath of the eye.
That deity which is in the earth is this very one, having taken hold of the downward breath (*apāna*) of a person;
that which is the space between [the earth and the atmosphere] is the equalizing breath (*samāna*);
and the wind is the pervasive breath (*vyāna*).
The Āditya (the Sun) is indeed well-known as the external vital breath (*prāṇa*) with respect to the deities; he rises, that is, he ascends.
For he favors this internal vital breath residing in the eye—the ocular *prāṇa*—by means of his light; the meaning is that he provides illumination for the eye so that forms may be perceived.

Likewise, the deity who is well-known as presiding over the earth takes hold of the son’s downward breath (*apāna*), that is, the function of *apāna*, drawing it in and bringing it under her control; she exists while bestowing favor by drawing [the breath] downwards.
This is the meaning.
Otherwise, the body would fall due to its weight, or it would rise up in the open space.
That wind which stays within—that is, in the middle of the space between heaven and earth—is called "space" (ākāśa).
It is like one situated on a bed;
the meaning is that it exists as the same [breath], sustaining the same [body].
This is because of its commonality with the intermediate space (*antarākāśa*) of the same [body].

And the intention is that whatever external wind exists in general, because of its commonality with pervasion (*vyāpti*), it functions as the pervasive air (*vyāna*), sustaining the *vyāna* [within the body]. //8//
The upward-breath (udāna) is indeed heat;
therefore, one whose heat has subsided [does not rise].
[He enters] into rebirth through the sense organs as they become integrated within the mind.
Or rather, that which is external and well-known as the common light— that light, in the body, favors the *udāna* [breath], meaning it favors the *udāna* wind through its own radiance.
Since the one who performs the departure (*utkrānti*) has the nature of light and is favored by external light, therefore, when an ordinary person’s light becomes extinguished—
meaning he is one whose natural light has been extinguished— [he departs].
Then one should know him to be one whose life is exhausted and who is about to die.
He attains a new existence, another body.
How? Together with the sense organs merging into the mind, as speech and the other organs enter [the mind]. (9)
With whatever thought he departs, by that very thought he enters the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The vital breath, joined with heat (*tejas*), together with the self (*ātman*), leads him to the world as it has been conceived.
With whatever state of mind one becomes possessed, by that very mind, through its conceptualization, one enters the *prāṇa*—the function of the chief vital breath—together with the sense organs.
The meaning is that at the time of death, having lost the functions of the senses, one remains solely through the function of the chief *prāṇa*.
Then the relatives say, "He breathes; he lives."

And that prāṇa, being joined with the function of udāna and united with the Self— the Lord, the enjoyer— being thus joined with the very function of udāna, leads and brings that enjoyer to the world according to his resolve and according to his desire, under the influence of his meritorious and sinful karma. //10//
He who, knowing thus, knows the vital breath—
his progeny does not perish, and he becomes immortal.
Regarding this, there is the following verse: PrUp 3.11.

Whoever, knowing thus, understands the vital breath (prāṇa) as distinguished by the aforementioned attributes such as its origin and so forth—for him this fruit is declared, both pertaining to this world and the next: his progeny, characterized by sons, grandsons, and so on, is never diminished or cut off;
and when the body has fallen away, through union with the vital breath, he becomes immortal, possessing the nature of immortality.
In this regard, there is this mantra-verse which expresses this matter in brief. //11//

One who understands the fivefold origin, arrival, location, pervasiveness, and the internal state of the vital breath (prāṇa) attains immortality; one who understands it attains immortality. Thus [ends] PrUp 3.12.

Having understood the origin of the supreme Self, the departure and arrival of the vital breath (prāṇa), its abiding and maintenance within this body through the actions of the mind, its sovereignty— like a sovereign emperor— over the various functions of the vital breaths established in five ways, and its manifestation externally in the form of the sun and other deities, and internally in the form of the eyes and other senses; having understood all this thus...
"One attains the immortal breath"—having understood this, the repetition "one attains the immortal" is for the purpose of completing the sense of the question. //12//

Thus ends the third question. The Fourth Question START PrUp 4.1: "Sir, what is that which is both beyond death and not beyond death? "My dear, as when one has put salt into water and, though one cannot perceive it by taking a sample, it is nevertheless there, being perceived by taste—thus, my dear, this great, endless, and infinite Reality is nothing but Consciousness alone. From this, indeed, beings arise; into this they set; and in this they live. "So it is, sir," said Śvetaketu. "But, my dear, you have not yet reached the point of understanding. "Please, sir, instruct me further. "As, my dear, one might lead a person away from the Gandhāra country with his eyes bound and leave him in a desolate place; and as he, crying out, 'I am lost! I am lost! would be wandering about in that desolate place, led by someone who then untied his bonds and told him, 'Friend, in this direction is the Gandhāra country; go toward it'; and as, following that instruction, he would by inquiry and questioning find his way to the Gandhāra country—just so, my dear, has this instruction been given to you. But there are no teachers of the Truth beyond this. "Sir, I am now ready for the final instruction. "My dear, as bees, seeking honey, gather from various trees and reduce their diverse juices to a single flavor, and as that honey is neither the same nor different from those juices; and as, my dear, if one were to taste it, one would know it to be sweet; even so, my dear, these creatures, though coming from this [Reality], do not know that 'We have come from here. Whatever they are in this world, whether tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gnat, or mosquito, they become that again. This [Reality] is indeed Brahman, the True. It is called Tadyo'yam ātmā (That which is this Self). This Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth, but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect. This body is mortal, held by death. By this is the immortal and bodiless Brahman veiled. 'The True,' they think, and they depart from here. Having reached the end of good deeds and the end of evil deeds, they enter the Supreme Light and appear in their own true form. He who has this knowledge becomes one with the True. There is a doubt regarding the man in the moon: 'Is he a human being? Or is he a gandharva? Or is he a god? Or is he a pitar? But he is truly a human being. As a caterpillar, having reached the tip of a blade of grass, draws itself across to another blade, so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, draws Himself across to another body. As a goldsmith takes apart an ornament and fashions another, newer and more beautiful than the first, so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, fashions for Himself another, newer and more beautiful form—whether of the ancestors, or of the gandharvas, or of the gods, or of Prajāpati, or of Brahmā, or of the [other] worlds. He becomes like those whose likeness he assumes. That which is the finest essence—this whole world has that as its soul. That is Reality. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Sir, please instruct me further. "My dear, as one might bring a person from the land of the Ābhīras, saying, 'This is your son, this is your father, this is your brother'; and as he, having been brought, would recognize them by their appearance and marks, saying, 'This is my father, this is my mother'; even so, my dear, this instruction has been given to you. But there are no teachers of the Truth beyond this. "Sir, I am now ready for the final instruction. "My dear, as when a man enters a dark place and does not perceive anything at all, so, my dear, is this mind within a person when it is unenlightened by the light of the Supreme Self. And as when a man enters a sunlit place after emerging from a dark prison and perceives everything clearly, so, my dear, is this mind within a person when it is enlightened by the light of the Supreme Self. As a razor placed in a razor-case is covered and cannot be found, but is found when the case is opened, so this mind is hidden in the cavity of the heart and is discovered through the syllable Om. As a metal vessel is covered by earth and, once uncovered, shines with its own luster, so this mind is covered by the sheath of ignorance and, when uncovered, shines with its own luster. As water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, so, my dear, the Self of the meditator and the Self of the meditated upon become one. As rivers flow toward the sea and, having reached it, lose their names and forms, so this person, freed from name and form, attains the Supreme, the Pure, the All-Pervading Consciousness. As a lump of salt, when thrown into water, dissolves and cannot be taken out again, yet the water, wherever tasted, is salty—so, my dear, this great, endless, and infinite Reality is nothing but Consciousness alone. Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya questioned him:
"Venerable sir, in this person, what things sleep? What things remain awake?"
"Which god, O King, is it that sees dreams? To whom does this pleasure belong? Upon what, indeed, are all things established? (PrU 4.1)
Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya questioned him.

Having completed the entire scope of the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) through three questions— namely, the transmigratory world consisting of the manifest realm, characterized by means and ends, and impermanent—

he now asked about that which is characterized by neither means nor ends, which is beyond the reach of breath and mind, which is a supersensuous object, auspicious, peaceful, unchanging, and imperishable.

It must be stated that Truth—which is accessible through supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*), designated as the Puruṣa, and which is unborn and both internal and external—is the subject of the answer to the three questions that now follow.
In this regard, it was stated in the second *Muṇḍaka* that from the supreme Imperishable (*akṣara*), like sparks from a well-kindled fire, all beings are born and into it they also merge.
What, then, are those "all beings" that are differentiated from the Imperishable?
How is it that, having become differentiated, they merge back into that very same place?
Or what are the characteristics of that syllable?
With the intention of explaining this, he now sets forth the questions:

"O Blessed One, in this person who possesses a head, hands, and so forth, which instruments sleep—meaning they undergo slumber and desist from their own functions? And which among them remain awake—meaning they maintain vigilance, the state of being without sleep, and perform their own functions? Which among these two, characterized as the body and the instruments, is this deity who sees dreams?
A dream, it is said, is that perception within the body, resembling waking, for one who has ceased from waking perception."
The intention [of the question] is this: are these brought about by a deity characterized as an effect (*kārya*), or by some [deity] characterized as an instrument (*karaṇa*)?
And when the activities of waking and dreaming have ceased, to whom does that serene, effortless, and unimpeded happiness belong?
At that time, having desisted from the activities of waking and dreaming, in what indeed are they all perfectly unified and established?
The meaning is that they become established together, like honey or like rivers and so forth that have entered the ocean, becoming inseparable from one another and incapable of distinction.

Now, it might be argued that this is logical because, having set aside their instruments such as the sickle, they cease from their own respective activities and remain each separately within themselves.
Why, then, does the questioner entertain the suspicion that the organs of sleeping persons undergo a state of unification in some single place?
The apprehension is indeed appropriate;

for since the organs are composite, exist for their own purposes, and are dependent during the waking state, it is logical that even in sleep they must be merged in something while remaining in a state of dependence due to their compositeness. Therefore, this question is precisely in accordance with that apprehension.

But here, for one who desires to know the specific nature of that aggregate of causes and effects in which [the self] is dissolved during deep sleep and at the time of cosmic dissolution—asking "What indeed might it be? and "In what are they all established?"—to him he said: To him he said: "O gentle one, it is this great, unborn Self (ātman), which is this [very] immortal and fearless Brahman. Fear arises from a second; for one who has no second, whence should fear come? He is the bridge, the support for keeping these worlds apart. Because they do not cross that bridge, these worlds do not collide. Therefore, the seers who have attained vision say: 'A gift is to be given, a sacrifice is to be performed, an oblation is to be offered,' thinking, 'Lest we fall into blind darkness. Blind darkness, indeed, they think they would fall into if they do not perform sacrifices and good works. Then there is the other world of those who have not sacrificed and have done no good works, a world full of blind darkness. Into that very [world] they go after death. But beyond this, there is another form of the Self, which is formless and is said to be immortal and fearless. It is like a flash of lightning in the clouds. As a flash of lightning illuminates everything, so too does that form illuminate everything. Those who meditate on this and depart from here, become of such a form after death. This is the form of the Self that is seen by those who possess knowledge. Thus he spoke. And thus far extends this instruction. Beyond this, there is only the teaching of the One without a second. For where there is a duality of "this" and "that," there one sees the other, one smells the other, one tastes the other, one speaks to the other, one hears the other, one thinks of the other, one touches the other, and one perceives the other. But where everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? By what and whom should one smell? By what and whom should one taste? By what and whom should one speak? By what and whom should one hear? By what and whom should one touch? By what and whom should one perceive? By what should one perceive Him by whom all this is perceived? By what, my dear, should one perceive the perceiver? Thus far, indeed, extends the instruction. "Beyond this, O venerable sir, there is something else.
