Just as, O Gārgya, all the rays of the sun, when it sets, become unified in this orb of light and emerge again and again when it rises,
even so, indeed, all that becomes unified in the supreme divine Mind.
Therefore, in that case, this person does not hear,
does not see,
and does not smell.
It does not taste; it does not touch;
it does not speak.
It does not take up;
it does not cause delight;
it does not emit.
It does not move;
they call it "sleeping. (PrU 4.2)
To him the teacher said: "Listen, O Gārgī, to that which you have asked.

Just as the rays of light—the beams of the sun—when the sun is setting and becoming invisible, all of them without exception become unified in this orb of light, which is a mass of radiance, reaching a state of non-distinction where they are no longer capable of being distinguished; such is the case with the rays of that very sun."
These [rays] spread out and are scattered as they rise up again and again from that which is rising.

Just as in this illustration, so indeed does all that collection of objects, senses, and so forth, [dissolve] into the supreme, most excellent, shining deity—the mind—because the deities of the eyes and other senses are dependent upon the mind; thus, the supreme deity is the mind, and into it [they dissolve] at the time of sleep.
It becomes one;
within the circle, it attains a state of non-distinction like a ray of light.
And for one who wishes to wake, the rays proceed from the circle solely by means of the mind and establish themselves for their own respective functions.

Because at the time of sleep, the ears and other organs— the instruments for perceiving sound and the rest— become, as it were, unified in the mind due to having ceased their respective functions; therefore, at that time of sleep, this person characterized as Devadatta and so forth does not hear,
does not see, does not smell, does not taste, does not touch, does not speak, does not take, and does not experience pleasure.
Ordinary people say that it emits, moves, and sleeps. //2//
In this city, the fires of the vital breaths (prāṇa) indeed remain awake. The apāna breath is indeed the Gārhapatya fire.
The Vyāna breath is the Anvāhāryapacana fire;
it is so called because it is led forth from the Gārhapatya fire.
The Āhavanīya fire is the Prāṇa breath.

While the instruments such as the ears and so forth are asleep, within this city—the body with its nine gates—the fires of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnayaḥ)—that is, the five winds themselves—remain awake like fires.

He states the commonality with fire: "This apāna is indeed the Gārhapatya fire. How so? He says: because from the Gārhapatya fire, at the time of the Agnihotra, the other fire, the Āhavanīya, is led forth; since it is led forth from it, the Gārhapatya fire is called the "praṇayana" (the source of leading forth).
Likewise, when one is asleep, the prāṇa moves through the mouth and nostrils as if being led by the apāna-vṛtti; therefore, prāṇa occupies the position of the Āhavanīya fire.
But because vyāna exits from the heart through the opening of the right channel and is thus connected with the southern direction, it is the Anvāhāryapacana, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. //3//
And here, the Hotṛ priest of the Agnihotra—
because he brings these two oblations, inhalation and exhalation, together equally— he is the Samāna.
The mind, indeed, is the sacrificer;
the upward breath (udāna) is the fruit of the sacrifice itself.
It leads this sacrificer day by day to Brahman.

Since exhalation and inhalation are like the two oblations of the *agnihotra*—because of their commonality as a pair—it is that wind which, acting as the *hotṛ* priest due to its role as the conductor of the two oblations, leads them equally (*samam*) for the sake of maintaining the body's existence;
what is that? It is the *samāna*.
Therefore, even the sleep of the wise man is indeed the offering of the Agnihotra;
thus, the intention is that one should consider the wise man not to be one who is without ritual action.
For it is said in the Vājasaneyaka: "Even while he sleeps, all beings are constantly searching for him."

For here, while the fires of the vital breaths (prāṇas) remain awake, one who desires to go to Brahman— like heaven, which is the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice— having withdrawn the external organs and their objects, is indeed the mind that remains awake as the sacrificer; for, like a sacrificer, it is predominant among the organs and instruments in its activity, and because it has set out toward Brahman as if toward heaven, the mind is conceived as the sacrificer.
The "desired fruit" is indeed the fruit of the sacrifice, which is the *udāna* breath;
for the attainment of the desired fruit occurs by means of the *udāna*.

How so? That *udāna*, having displaced the sacrificer—designated as the mind—from even the state of dreaming, leads him day after day at the time of deep sleep to the imperishable Brahman, as if to heaven.
Therefore, the *udāna* stands in the place of the fruit of the sacrifice. //4//

Thus, for the one who knows, from the time the ear and other senses cease until he awakens from sleep, there is only the experience of the fruits of all sacrifices; it is not for his detriment as it is for the ignorant. In this way, the state of being a knower is praised. For it is not that the ears and other senses alone sleep while the fires of the vital breaths (prāṇas) remain awake for the knower; rather, the mind—which experiences independence during both waking and dreaming—daily attains deep sleep. Since the transition through waking, dreaming, and deep sleep occurs in turn equally for all living beings, this praise of the state of being a knower is indeed appropriate.
Regarding what was asked— "Which god is it that sees dreams?"— he says:
"In this state, this god experiences his own majesty in a dream."
Whatever has been seen, he perceives as something already seen;
whatever has been heard, he hears again as something already heard; and whatever has been experienced in various places and directions, he experiences it again and again.
He sees all—the seen and the unseen, the heard and the unheard, the perceived and the unperceived, the real and the unreal;
everyone sees. (PrU 4.5)

While the ears and other senses have ceased their activity, yet while the vital breaths (prāṇa) and other airs remain awake for the protection of the body, in this interval prior to the attainment of deep sleep, this deity— having withdrawn the instruments such as the ears into its own self like the rays of the sun— experiences and attains in the dream state "greatness," that is, its own power consisting of the manifestation of various states of being characterized by objects and subjects.

[Objection: Surely the mind is the instrument for the experiencer’s experience of greatness; how then can it be said that he experiences it independently? For the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is indeed independent. [Reply: This is not a fault, because the independence of the Knower of the Field is produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the mind. For the Knower of the Field does not, in the ultimate sense, sleep or wake of his own accord. It has been stated in the *Vājasaneyaka* that his waking and dreaming are produced solely by the limiting adjunct of the mind: “For he, having become as if in a dream, thinks, as it were, and moves about, as it were” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7), and so forth.
Therefore, it is entirely logical to state that the mind possesses independence in the experience of its own manifestations.

As for the claim made by some— that if the mind were accompanied by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the self-luminosity (*svayaṃ-jyotiṣṭva*) of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) during the time of dreaming would be contradicted—
that is an error caused by their failure to understand the meaning of the scripture.

Because even all empirical usage such as self-luminosity and so forth, which persists until liberation, belongs solely to the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*) and is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the mind; for [the Upaniṣads state]:

"But where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32); "But there is for him contact with the objects of perception" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14); and "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
14) From such scriptural passages as these, this doubt belongs only to those of dull understanding regarding Brahman, and not to those who know the one Self.
[Objection: But if this is so, then [it contradicts the scripture]: "In this state, this person is self-luminous" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.28).
14) Thus, the qualification would be meaningless.

To this it is replied: what you say is far too little; for if [the Self] were confined within the heart—as in the passage, "He lies in that space which is within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17)—then its self-luminosity would be all the more contradicted.
If it is argued: "True, this defect may indeed exist; however, since in the dream state [the self] exists solely as self-luminous (*svayañjyotiṣ*), at least half of the burden is removed," we say:

no. Even there, because of the scriptural statement, "He lies in the *purītat* (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19)," the person remains connected to the *purītat* channels; therefore, the intention that half the burden is removed by the person's self-luminosity even in that state is likewise false.
How then is it that [the scripture] says, "In this regard, this person is self-luminous" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14)?
If it is argued that this scriptural statement is to be disregarded because it belongs to a different recensional branch (śākhā), we say no;
for the oneness [of the Self] is what is intended, since the single Self is indeed the meaning sought to be made known and desired to be understood by all the Vedāntas.
Therefore, it is logical to state that the self's nature as self-luminous is established even in dream, because the Śruti reveals the reality of things exactly as they are.

If this is so, then listen to the meaning of the Śruti, setting aside all preconceptions; for the meaning of the Śruti cannot be understood—even in a hundred years—by anyone who merely fancies themselves a scholar while remaining under the sway of such preconceptions.

Just as when one sleeps in the space of the heart, in the pericardium, or in the channels, the Self can be shown as distinct from those because of the absence of connection with them— and thus its self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) is not contradicted— so too, in the mind which is filled with latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arisen from ignorance, desire, and action, the seer who is completely detached from all effects and instruments perceives himself as other than the latent impressions that take the form of objects, seeing through ignorance another entity as it were, while the latent impressions arise from the cause of karma. Thus, by virtue of being distinct from the latent impressions whose nature is the visible, [the Self's self-luminosity remains uncontradicted].
The self-luminous nature [of the Self] cannot be denied even by an extremely arrogant logician.
Therefore, it has been well said: "When the organs have dissolved into the mind, but the mind itself has not yet dissolved, one who consists of mind (manomaya) sees dreams.

How does he experience his greatness? It is explained: whatever friend or even son was previously seen, being permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those, he perceives—arising from the impressions of sons, friends, and so forth—a son or a friend as if they were present.
One thinks, "I see by means of knowledge.

Likewise, one hears a previously heard object as if hearing it again through its latent impression (*vāsanā*). And through ignorance, one repeatedly re-experiences what was experienced in other places and other directions—that is, in other regions and other quarters—as well as what was seen in this life and what was not seen but was seen in another birth. This is the meaning.
Because a latent impression (*vāsanā*) cannot arise for that which has never been seen before;
thus, "what was heard and what was not heard, what was experienced and what was not experienced in this life by the mind alone" means that which was experienced by the mind alone in another birth.
And "the real" (*sat*) refers to water and so forth as they exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Unreal things such as a mirage or water in a desert;

what need is there for further elaboration? Being conditioned by all mental latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the god of the mind—the self of all instruments—sees all things and sees everything in this way during dreams. //5//
When he is overcome by heat,
then this deity does not see dreams.
Then, at that time, this happiness arises in this body.
When that deity in the form of the mind is completely overwhelmed by the solar heat known as bile residing in the channels—
such that the gateway of its latent impressions (vāsanās) is obscured— and when the rays of the mind, along with the organs of perception, are withdrawn into the heart;
when the mind, like fire within wood, remains pervading the entire body in the form of undifferentiated consciousness, then it is in a state of deep sleep (suṣupta).
At this time, this deity called "mind" does not perceive dreams due to the brilliance of the gateway of perception.
Then, at that moment, there arises in this body this bliss—the meaning is that consciousness becomes unobstructed, pervading the body without distinction, and serene. // 6 //
At this time, the organs and their functions, which are bound by ignorance, desire, and karma, become stilled.

When they have been stilled, the nature of the Self—which was previously perceived as otherwise due to limiting adjuncts—becomes non-dual, one, auspicious, and peaceful. To demonstrate this very state through the penetration of the mere products of ignorance such as earth and so forth, he provides an illustration:
Just as, my dear, birds settle upon a tree for shelter,
even so, indeed, all this settles in the Supreme Self.

That illustration is as follows: just as, my dear Priyadarśana, birds go toward a tree for the sake of dwelling—a "dwelling-tree"—even so, indeed, according to that illustration, all this which is about to be described is established in the supreme Self, the Imperishable. //7//
What is all that?
Earth and the subtle essence of earth.
Water and the subtle element of water; fire and the subtle element of fire;
air and the subtle element of air.
Space and the mere dimension of space;
the eye and the visible;
the ear and the audible.
The nose and the object of smell; the tongue and the object of taste;
the skin and the object of touch.
Speech and that which is to be spoken; the hands and that which is to be grasped; the sexual organ and that which is to be delighted.
The anus and that which is to be excreted;
the feet and that which is to be traversed; the mind and that which is to be thought.
Intellect and that which is to be known;
the ego and that which is to be made an object of the ego;
the mind and that which is to be perceived.
The radiance must be made to shine forth,
and the vital breath must be sustained.

Earth is gross and possesses five qualities; its cause is the earth-element (pṛthivīmātrā), which is the subtle element of odor (gandhatanmātra). Likewise, there is water and the water-element, as well as fire and the fire-element.
Wind and the subtle element of wind, space and the subtle element of space; this means the gross and the subtle elements.
Likewise, the eye and visible forms, the ear and sounds, and the nose and odors are to be regarded [as such].
Taste and that which is to be tasted, the skin and that which is to be touched, and speech and that which is to be spoken.
The hands and that which is to be grasped; the organ of generation and that which is to be delighted; the anus and that which is to be excreted.
The feet and that which is to be traversed,
as well as the organs of cognition and the organs of action as previously described,
and the mind as mentioned before.
That which is to be deliberated upon has that [object] as its domain; intellect is of the nature of ascertainment, and that which is to be understood has that [object] as its domain.
The ego (ahaṅkāra) is the internal organ characterized by self-conceit, and that which is to be identified as "I" is its object;
the mind (citta) is the internal organ possessed of consciousness, and that which is to be cognized is its object.
And *tejas* (heat/light) is that which, distinct from the sense-organ of touch, is the object to be manifested and illuminated by the skin characterized by light;

and *prāṇa* is the "thread" (*sūtra*)—as they call it—by which everything must be held together and woven, for the entire aggregate of effects and instruments, consisting of name and form, is joined together solely for the sake of another; this much alone is it. //8//
Now, that which is the supreme nature of the Self, having entered here as an enjoyer and an agent— like the sun reflected in water and so forth—
is this very one: the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer, the person consisting of consciousness (*vijñānātman*).
He becomes firmly established in the supreme, imperishable Self.

For this is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, and the agent; it is the "self of consciousness" (*vijñānātman*). "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*), which are called "consciousness" in the sense that "by means of them one is conscious"; however, this [self] is "consciousness" in the sense that "it itself is conscious," being thus the agent and the form of action.
It is the self of that, meaning its very nature is that of the knower.
The *puruṣa* is so called because he is filled with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the aggregate of the body and the organs;
and he is established in the supreme Self, the support of the world, which is the eye, just as the reflection of the sun in water and the like returns to its source, the sun itself. //9//
He states the fruit for one who knows that oneness:
he attains the supreme Imperishable itself.
He who, my dear, knows that which is shadowless, bodiless, bloodless, radiant, and imperishable—he becomes all this, he becomes everything.
Regarding this, there is this verse: Prasna Upaniṣad 4.10.
It is said that one attains the supreme imperishable (akṣara), which possesses the characteristics about to be described:
he who, indeed, is liberated from all desires, [attains] that which is shadowless and free from darkness, bodiless and devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as name and form.
It is "alo hita" (bloodless), being devoid of all qualities such as redness; because it is thus, it is "śubhra" (brilliant) and "śuddha" (pure);
and because it is free from all specific attributes, it is "akṣara" (the imperishable).

O gentle one, he who, having renounced everything, perceives— that is, knows— the Reality called Puruṣa, which is without vital breath, beyond the range of mind, auspicious, tranquil, devoid of exterior or interior, and unborn— he is omniscient; for nothing whatsoever remains unknown to him.
Previously, through ignorance, he was omniscient; then, when ignorance is removed by knowledge, he becomes the All.
Regarding that matter, this verse serves as a mantra, summarizing the meaning already stated. //10//

"Where the conscious self, along with all the gods, the vital breaths, and all beings, find their support—that Imperishable, my dear, he who knows it is all-knowing; he has entered into everything. (PrUp 4.11)

The conscious self, together with the deities such as Agni and others, the vital breaths, the senses beginning with sight, and the elements such as earth and the rest—these all find their support and enter into that Imperishable (akṣara) wherein they abide; O gentle Priyadarśana, he who knows that Imperishable is omniscient, for it is He who has entered into everything, meaning He pervades all. //11//
Thus ends the fourth question.
The Fifth Question START PrUp 5.1: "Sir, what is that through which, when it is known, everything here becomes known?
Then Śaibya Satyakāma asked him:
"Venerable sir, if someone among men should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* until the end of his life,
which world indeed does he win by that?"
Then Śaibya Satyakāma questioned him. Now, with the desire to prescribe the meditation on the syllable *oṃ* as the means for attaining both the higher and lower Brahman, the inquiry begins:
"O Venerable One, whoever among men—this being something like a marvel—[practices it] until the end of his departure, that is, until death, throughout his entire life," so much is the sense.
"One should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ*," that is, one should contemplate it directly;
having withdrawn the senses from external objects, with a concentrated mind, and with the state of Brahman infused through devotion into the *oṃ*,

the meaning of the term "meditation" (*abhidhyāna*) is the uninterrupted continuity of the cognition of the Self, not interrupted by any other heterogeneous cognitions, resembling the flame of a lamp in a windless place.

Supported by numerous restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), such as truthfulness, celibacy, non-violence, non-possessiveness, renunciation, withdrawal, purity, contentment, and freedom from deceit, he thus maintains his vow for as long as he lives.
Among the many worlds that exist to be conquered through various forms of knowledge and action—which world indeed does he conquer by means of that meditation on the syllable *Oṃ*? //1//
To him he said:
"Satyakāma, this syllable *oṃ* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman."
Therefore, the wise man follows one or the other by means of this very abode.

To him who had thus questioned, Pippalāda said: "O Satyakāma, this indeed is both the higher and the lower Brahman. The higher Brahman is Truth, called the Imperishable (Akṣara), designated as the Puruṣa; and the lower is that which is called Prāṇa, the first-born. That [Brahman] is indeed the syllable Om, having the nature of Om because it has Om as its symbol.

For the higher Brahman is beyond being characterized by sound and other qualities, and is devoid of all specific attributes; therefore, because it lies within the domain of the supersensuous, it cannot be fathomed by the mind alone."

It is understood from the authority of the scriptures that when the syllable *oṃ*—which serves as the locus for images of Viṣṇu and other deities—is infused with the nature of Brahman through devotion, it becomes propitious to those who meditate upon it; and so too does the higher Brahman. Therefore, the higher and the lower Brahman are metaphorically designated as the syllable *oṃ*. Consequently, one who knows this follows and attains either the higher or the lower Brahman by means of this very meditation on *oṃ*, which is the instrument for attaining the Self; for *oṃ* is the nearest support for Brahman.
If he should meditate upon a single measure,
being made conscious by that very [measure], he very quickly attains the world of the living beings (jagatī).
The Ṛgvedic verses lead him to the world of men;
there, endowed with austerity, celibacy, and faith, he experiences greatness.
Even if he does not know the division of all the *mātrās* of the syllable *oṃ*, nevertheless, by the power of meditating on *oṃ*, he goes to a distinguished state.
Due to the deficiency of knowing only a portion of it, one who takes refuge in *oṃ* does not go to an evil state even if he has fallen away from both ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
What then? Even if he knows only a single *mātrā* of *oṃ*, if he should meditate on that single *mātrā* alone—
Always meditating, he— perceived and awakened by that very meditation on the single-syllabled *oṃkāra*— very quickly, in an instant, attains [the state] in the world, that is, on the earth; indeed,
the world of men.
For many births indeed occur in the world;
therein, they lead that practitioner, bringing him near, to the very human world within the world.
Thus, being born there in a human life as a foremost among the twice-born, he is endowed with austerity, celibacy, and faith.
One who has lost faith does not experience greatness or power; acting according to his own whims, he who has fallen from yoga never at any time goes to an evil state. //3//
Now, if he is united with the mind by means of the two measures,
he is led up to the intermediate space by the *yajus* formulas to the world of Soma.
Having experienced splendor in the world of Soma, he returns once again.

Furthermore, if one who knows the division of two measures should meditate upon the form of Oṃ as distinguished by two measures— upon that which consists of thought (manas), whose nature is dream, which consists of the Yajus, and has Soma as its deity— he becomes unified with it and attains identity through one-pointedness. Having thus become unified and having died, he is led up by the Yajus-mantras, which consist of the second measure, to the intermediate space (antarikṣa), which is the support of the second measure and takes the form of the second measure.

The meaning is that the *yajus* formulas cause one to attain a gentle birth in the world of Soma; having experienced enjoyment there in the world of Soma, he returns again toward the world of men. //4//
Furthermore, he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable "Om" consisting of three measures— he,
having attained union with the heat in the sun, [proceeds further].
Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he freed from evil. Led upward by the Sāmans, he goes to the world of Brahman.
From this mass of living beings, he beholds the Person who dwells within the city and is both higher and lower. Regarding this, there are these two verses: PrUp_5.5 //

Furthermore, he who meditates upon this syllable *oṃ*—which consists of three morae (*trimātra*) and is distinguished by a consciousness whose object is those three morae—by means of this very syllable *oṃ* as a symbol (*pratīka*) upon the Supreme Person situated within the sun; by that meditation, [he attains his goal].

For it is the nature of the syllable *oṃ* to serve as a support (*ālambana*) by way of being a symbol, since otherwise the scriptural declarations of non-difference—such as "the higher and the lower Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4)—and the repeated use of the accusative case in the word "the syllable *oṃ*" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2) would be contradicted.

Although it is logical that the third *mātrā* functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the third meditation, nevertheless, in accordance with the context, it must be understood as the accusative case alone—as in "the supreme Person consisting of three *mātrās"—following the maxim: "One should sacrifice the individual for the sake of the family" (Mahābhārata 3.187.17).

That [meditator], consisting of the form of the third *mātrā*, becomes merged in the light of the sun while meditating; even after death, he does not return—not like those going to the world of the Moon and so forth—but rather at the very moment he has become merged in the sun.

Just as a footless serpent is liberated from its skin and, once freed from that worn-out skin, becomes new again; even so, this person— according to the illustration— is liberated from evil, which stands in the place of the serpent’s skin and consists of impurity,
and is led upward by the Sāman chants, whose forms consist of the third measure, to the world of Brahman, the world of Hiraṇyagarbha, known as Satya.
That Hiraṇyagarbha is the self of all transmigrating individual souls;
for he is the inner self of all beings in the form of the subtle body (liṅga),
since all individual souls are gathered within that subtle-body-self.
Therefore, he is a mass of life-force (*jīvaghana*).

That wise man, proficient in the *oṃkāra* consisting of three measures, beholds—while meditating—the Puruṣa known as the Supreme Self, who is higher than the highest, higher than this *jīvaghana* which is Hiraṇyagarbha; he sees him dwelling in the city (*puriśaya*), having entered into all bodies.
Therefore, there are two mantras that illuminate this aforementioned meaning. //5//
There are three measures subject to death, employed one after another, mutually joined and not separated from one another.
When these— external, internal, and intermediate— are properly applied in ritual actions, the knower does not tremble.

The three morae of the syllable *oṃ*—namely those called *a*, *u*, and *m*—are "possessing death," meaning they possess death; that is to say, they have not transcended the sphere of death and remain within the sphere of death. These are employed in the acts of meditation upon the Self, and furthermore, they are mutually attached, being interconnected with one another.

"Non-detached" (*anaviprayuktā*) means specifically engaged with each individual object, whereas "detached" (*viprayuktā*) refers to those not so engaged; "non-non-detached" (*anaviprayuktā*) means neither detached nor non-detached.

What then? It refers specifically to the time of meditation when one is engaged in the three activities—external, internal, and intermediate—characterized by the contemplation of a person in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

When the practices of yoga are correctly applied— that is, when they are employed at the time of right meditation— the yogi who knows the divisions of the syllable *oṃ* as described does not tremble and does not waver; for such a knower, movement is not possible.

Since the persons of the waking, dreaming, and deep-sleep states, together with their respective locations, are seen as being of the nature of the three measures (mātrās) and as having the form of the syllable Om, he who knows this—having become the Self of all and consisting of Om—how could he move, or from where, or toward what? //6//

The second mantra is for the purpose of summarizing all meanings: By means of the *ṛg* verses this [earth], by means of the *yajus* formulas the intermediate space, and that which the seers know through the *sāman* chants— START PrUp 5.7.
The wise one follows that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme, by means of the very abode that is the syllable Om. (PrU 5.7)
By means of the *ṛc*s, they know this world characterized by humans;
by means of the *yajus* formulas, the intermediate space presided over by Soma;
and by means of the *sāman* chants, that which is the world of Brahman—the third—only the wise, the intelligent, and the learned perceive it, not those who are ignorant.
The wise person, by means of the *oṃkāra* as a means of realization, follows and attains that threefold world characterized as the lower Brahman.

By that very *oṃkāra*, he reaches that which is the supreme Brahman— the imperishable, the truth, called the Puruṣa, which is peaceful and liberated, devoid of all distinctions such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and because of that, undecaying (free from old age) and immortal (free from death).
Because it is free from the transformation of old age, it is fearless; and because it is fearless, it is supreme and unsurpassed.
The meaning is that one follows that [supreme state] by means of the syllable *oṃ* as its abode and the instrument of attainment.
The word "iti" serves the purpose of indicating the completion of the sentence. //7//

Then Sukeśa Bhāradvāja asked him:
"Venerable sir, Prince Hiraṇyanābha of Kosala approached me and asked this question:
'O Bhāradvāja, do you know the Person of sixteen parts?'"
I said to that youth, "I do not know this.
If I had known this, why would I not have told you?
Truly, he who speaks untruth withers away, root and all.
"Therefore, I ought not to speak a falsehood.
He mounted his chariot in silence and departed.
Then Sukeśa Bhāradvāja questioned him:

It has been stated that the entire world, characterized by cause and effect together with the individual self (vijñānātman), becomes established in the supreme Imperishable during the state of deep sleep.
By implication, it is established that at the time of dissolution as well, the world becomes established in that very same Imperishable and arises from that alone.
For it is not possible for an effect to be established without a cause;

and it has been stated that "this vital breath is born from the Self. Furthermore, the settled conclusion of all the Upaniṣads is that the supreme good arises from the thorough knowledge of that which is the root of the world.

Immediately following that, it was stated, "He becomes all-knowing and everything"; however, it must be explained where that imperishable reality, called the Puruṣa, is to be known. To that end, this question is commenced, and there is also a recapitulation of what has occurred in order to demonstrate the difficulty of attaining such knowledge, so that those seeking liberation may apply themselves with special effort toward its acquisition. "O Blessed One, a prince named Hiraṇyanābha, born in Kosala—thus a Kausalya—and by birth a Kṣatriya, approached me and asked this very question now being stated."
"O Bhāradvāja, do you know that person who consists of sixteen parts—that is, that person in whom there are sixteen parts (kalās), like limbs, which are forms superimposed upon the Self by ignorance?
To that prince, the young boy who had questioned me, I said: 'I do not know this person about whom you ask.'"

Even though I had spoken thus, he remained unable to conceive that I was ignorant; therefore, I stated the reason for my ignorance: "If I had somehow known this man about whom you asked—meaning, if I had understood him—how could I not have told you, who are so exceedingly endowed with the qualities of a disciple and who are a petitioner? 'I did not tell' (nāvakṣyam) means 'I did not speak,' or 'I would not speak. Perceiving once more that he seemed to lack conviction, I spoke again in order to convince him."

He who, being one thing, represents himself as otherwise, speaking what is false—that is, a matter contrary to reality—is "rooted out," meaning he withers away along with his very root; he is cut off from both this world and the next, and perishes.
Since this is so, I ought not to speak untruth like a fool.

Having been thus convinced, that prince, silent and ashamed, mounted his chariot and departed just as he had come. Therefore, this is established: knowledge must be spoken only to one who has approached according to the rule and is a fit vessel; and falsehood must not be spoken under any circumstances whatsoever. I ask you, O Puruṣa, about that person who dwells within me like a thorn in my heart—where does that person to be known abide? //1//
To him he said:
"Right here within the body, my dear, is that person in whom these sixteen parts originate."
To him he said:

"Right here within the body, in the midst of the space within the lotus of the heart, O dear one, that person is to be known—not in another place—in which these sixteen parts, beginning with breath, which are about to be described, originate and arise; thus, by means of these sixteen parts."

The partless Puruṣa is perceived as if possessed of parts through ignorance (*avidyā*) by means of those [factors] that have become limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); therefore, it is stated that the parts originate from Him, so that by removing the superimposition caused by those adjuncts, that Puruṣa may be shown in His absolute isolation through knowledge (*vidyā*). For indeed, in the case of the utterly undifferentiated, non-dual, and pure Reality, the conventional usage of teaching and learning cannot be carried out without superimposition; thus, the origin, persistence, and dissolution of the parts [are described].
Objects of ignorance are superimposed [upon consciousness].
For the constituent powers (kalās), while never being distinct from pure consciousness, are observed at all times as they arise, persist, and dissolve.

Therefore, some deluded people maintain that consciousness itself arises and perishes every moment in the form of jars and other objects, just as clarified butter [solidifies] through contact with fire.
Others hold that upon its cessation, everything becomes as if empty.

Others maintain that consciousness, which has objects such as jars as its domain, arises and perishes as something impermanent belonging to the eternal self who is the cognizer. The Lokāyatikas assert that consciousness is a property of the primary elements (*bhūta*).

The Self alone—consciousness whose nature is free from birth and destruction—is manifested through the attributes of limiting adjuncts such as name and form; as it is said: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), "Brahman is Consciousness" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 5.3), and "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).

28) From such scriptural passages as "a mere mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12), since consciousness does not deviate among objects that do deviate in their own nature, in whatever manner and whichever object is cognized, by the very fact of being known in that way, each and every one of those objects possesses the non-deviation of consciousness.
It is also untenable to claim that some reality exists yet is not known, just as one might say, "form is seen, but the eye does not exist.
However, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) may deviate [from its cognition], whereas knowledge never deviates from the object;
for even in the absence of one object of knowledge, knowledge persists because it exists with respect to another object of knowledge.
For there is no such thing as an object of knowledge for anyone in the absence of cognition, since it is not perceived during deep sleep.
If it is argued that, because cognition also is absent during deep sleep—just like the object of knowledge—the nature of cognition itself is subject to deviation, we say: no.

Since cognition, which illuminates the object of knowledge, acts as its manifestor like light, the absence of the manifestor (cognition) would be impossible in the absence of the manifested (the object), just as the absence of light is impossible in the absence of the illuminated; thus, the existence of consciousness in deep sleep is not untenable.
For it is not possible for a nihilist (vaināśika) to conceive of the non-existence of the eye simply because forms are not perceived by the eye in darkness.
If it is argued that the nihilist indeed conceives of the non-existence of cognition when there is an absence of an object of cognition,
then the nihilist must explain by what means the non-existence of that [cognition] itself is conceived.
If it is argued that because non-existence is also an object of knowledge, its occurrence is impossible in the absence of cognition—

and that since cognition is not distinct from its object, there is no cognition when there is no object— this is not so; for since non-existence is also admitted to be an object of knowledge, the nihilists (Vaināśikas) must admit that even non-existence is an object of knowledge and is eternal.

If cognition were conceived as eternal and non-different from that [object], then since the absence of that object would consist of the nature of cognition itself, its status as an "absence" would be a mere matter of words and not an actual state of absence; furthermore, cognition would be impermanent.
Moreover, nothing is lost by merely superimposing the name "absence" upon eternal cognition.

If it is argued that even though non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of cognition (*jñeya*), it is distinct from cognition, then it follows that there is no absence of cognition when there is an absence of the object of cognition.
If it is further argued that the object of cognition is distinct from cognition, but cognition is not distinct from the object of cognition; [we reply: ...
This is not so, because it is a mere matter of words and no distinction can be established.

If the identity of the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself is accepted, then the claim that "the object of knowledge is not distinct from knowledge" and "knowledge is not distinct from the object of knowledge" is merely verbal, just as it would be if one were to accept that "fire is not distinct from flame" and "flame is not distinct from fire."
But if knowledge were distinct from the object of knowledge, then it would be established that in the absence of an object of knowledge, the absence of knowledge is impossible.
If it is argued that knowledge does not exist in the absence of an object because it is not observed, we say no; for consciousness is admitted to exist even in deep sleep.
For the nihilists (vaināśikas) indeed maintain that consciousness exists even in deep sleep.
If it is argued that even there, consciousness is admitted to be an object of cognition by itself,
we say no, because the distinction [between subject and object] is established.

For it is established that for a cognition whose object is to be known as non-existent, there is a difference between the knowledge and the object of knowledge because the object of knowledge is distinct from the non-existence [it cognizes].
Indeed, once that is established, it cannot be made otherwise—even by hundreds of Nihilists—to bring it back to life like a dead man.
If you argue that this leads to an infinite regress in your own position—where the knowability of a cognition would require another cognition, and that another, and so on—[we reply: no.
No, because for one who knows everything, such a division is logically possible.

For when all that is knowable belongs to someone, then cognition distinct from that [knowable] is admitted by the nihilist (*vaināśika*) to be nothing but cognition itself; thus, only a second division is accepted, and not a third consisting of an object thereof, so there is no possibility of an infinite regress.
If it is argued that if cognition were not cognizable by itself, its omniscience would be lost—[we reply: no.
Let that fault belong to him alone; what need have we for its refutation?

Furthermore, there is the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) because cognition must itself be an object of knowledge. And for the Nihilists (vaināśika), cognition must necessarily be an object of knowledge.
Furthermore, because it would not be cognizable by itself, an infinite regress would be unavoidable.
If it is argued that this same fault applies equally [to our position], we say no; for the unity of cognition is logically established.

Knowledge is one and the same, existing in all places, times, persons, and states; it appears as manifold due to the diversity of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as name and form, like the reflection of the sun and other objects in water and so forth. Therefore, this is not a fault.
Accordingly, it is said here:
"But [it is argued] that according to the scripture, the Person (*puruṣa*) is limited right here within the body, like a jujube fruit in a bowl."
No, because [the Self] is the cause of the parts such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
for one could not conceive that something limited merely to the body could be the cause of the parts such as the vital breath, faith, and so forth;
moreover, the body itself is an effect of those parts.
For the body, which is the effect of the arts that are the human activities, could not contain within itself its own cause—the person—just as a jujube fruit contains the bowl [in which it was grown].
If it is argued that this would be like the case of a seed and a tree:

just as a tree, which is the effect of a seed, and its effect, the fruit (such as a mango), contain within themselves the seed which is their own cause’s cause; so too the body, though it is the cause’s cause of the person, might contain the person within itself.
If [it is argued that they are the same], no; because they are different and because they possess parts.

In the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the seeds enclosed within the tree's fruit are indeed other than the causal seed; however, in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), that very same person, who is the cause of his own cause, is heard of as being internalized within the body.

Furthermore, because seeds, trees, and so forth possess constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*), they may have the relationship of container and contained; however, the *puruṣa* is partless (*niravayava*), whereas the *kalās*, the body, and so on, do possess parts.
By this same reasoning, it is untenable for even space (*ākāśa*) to be the support of the body, let alone for the *puruṣa*, which is the cause of space. Therefore, the illustration is not analogous.
If it is argued, "What is the use of an illustration? It could be so by virtue of scriptural statement," [the response follows].
No, because speech is not a causal agent;
for speech does not operate toward the alteration of a thing.
What then? It illuminates the object exactly as it is.
Therefore, this statement "within the body" should be understood as being like [the phrase] "the space within the egg.
Furthermore, because he is the cause of perception—
since the Puruṣa is perceived through the marks of seeing, hearing, thinking, and discerning, as if delimited within the body— he is therefore said to be "within the body, my dear."

Thus, even a fool would not wish to say—even in his mind—that the Self, being the cause of space, is limited by the body like a jujube fruit in a bowl; how much less so could the authoritative Śruti say such a thing? //2//

It has been stated that "in whom these sixteen parts originate," which was said for the purpose of qualifying the Puruṣa; however, since that origin of the parts is also heard of in another context, it is now stated— in what sequence does it occur?— and for this purpose, namely, to show that creation is preceded by consciousness.
He reflected:
"Upon whose departure shall I depart? And upon whose being established shall I be established? (PrU 6.3)

That person consisting of sixteen parts was questioned by Bhāradvāja; he, who is "one who has seen" (*īkṣitṛ*), meaning he performed the act of seeing—namely, regarding the sequence of the fruits of creation and so forth.
How so? It is said: "In what specific agent, having departed from the body, shall I depart?
Or in what body, being established, shall I be established?"—that is, where shall I abide once established.
He created the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
From the vital breath, he created faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, the mind, food; from food, vigor, austerity, sacred formulas, action, the worlds, and in the worlds, name.
Now, it may be argued that the Self (ātman) is not the agent, but rather primordial matter (pradhāna) is the agent;

therefore, having taken up the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha), the pradhāna proceeds to evolve in the form of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth. In this regard, the following is untenable: the assertion of the Spirit’s agency as being independent and preceded by volition (īkṣā).

Since the *pradhāna*—in which the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* are in equilibrium—is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as the creator of creation; or since atoms exist that follow the will of a Lord (*īśvara*); and because there is no evidence for the self’s agency given its unity, and because it is impossible for the self to be the author of its own misfortune within itself—a conscious being would not intentionally produce misfortune for itself through a deliberate act.

Therefore, when the non-intelligent *pradhāna* proceeds according to a fixed sequence as if preceded by deliberation (*īkṣā*) for the sake of the human goal, there is this figurative attribution of intelligence to it—as in "it deliberated" (*sa īkṣāñcakre*) and so forth—just as one says "the king" with respect to a servant who accomplishes all the king's purposes.
[Reply: No, because agency is as possible for the Self as its status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

Just as for the Sāṃkhya, the self—which is pure consciousness and non-transforming—possesses the status of an enjoyer, so too for the proponents of the Veda, the agency of the world preceded by [the power of] seeing and so forth is established through the authority of the Śruti.
The transformation into another state of being would entail impermanence, impurity, and multiplicity for the self; however, this is not a modification of its nature as pure consciousness.

Therefore, while for you the enjoyership of the Puruṣa within its own self is merely a modification of the nature of pure consciousness and does not constitute a fault, for you Vedic proponents it is likewise acceptable.

If it is argued that, in the case of being the creator of the world, there would necessarily be a transformation into another ontological principle (*tattvāntara-pariṇāma*), which would entail all defects such as the impermanence of the Self, we say: no. For even though the Self is one, we accept that distinctions are produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—whether with or without adjuncts—within the context of ignorance (*avidyā*). Indeed, a distinction produced by the limiting adjuncts of name-and-form created by ignorance is accepted for the sake of the conventional usage established by the scriptures concerning the bondage and liberation of the Self, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).

And that reality which is unconditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—the one without a second, the object of attainment, unfathomable by the intellects of all logicians, fearless, and auspicious—is accepted [as the truth].
In that state, there can be no agency, no enjoyership, nor action, instrument, or fruit, because of the non-duality (advaita) of all existents.

However, the Sāṃkhyas, having postulated that agency, action, instruments, and fruit are merely superimposed upon the Puruṣa by ignorance (avidyā), tremble again before this [truth], as they have strayed outside the sacred tradition (āgama).

Desiring that the state of being an enjoyer belongs to the *puruṣa* only in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), and postulating a *pradhāna* as a distinct principle that is itself an ultimately real entity beyond the *puruṣa*, those who are objects of the intellect fashioned by other logicians come to grief;
likewise, other logicians are confounded by the Sāṃkhyas.

Thus, because they conceive of mutually contradictory meanings—like living beings seeking material gain who perceive objects of their own conflicting pride—they are drawn far away from the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārthatattva*). Therefore, disregarding those views, we shall briefly point out the defects in the systems of the logicians so that seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), being intent upon the vision of unity which is the true meaning of the Vedānta, may become devoted to it; however, this is not done with the same thoroughness as the logicians themselves.
Therefore, it has been said here:
"Having entrusted the cause of the arising of conflict to those very people who are disputing,
the knower of the Vedas, his true wisdom protected by them, attains peace and is extinguished in bliss."
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, no distinction can be established between the two modifications of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and being an agent (*kartṛtva*).

What indeed is this modification characterized as "being an enjoyer" that is of a different genus from "being an agent," such that the Puruṣa is postulated as the enjoyer alone and not the agent, while Pradhāna is the agent alone and not the enjoyer?
But was it not said that the Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone, and while remaining established in his own self, he undergoes modification when experiencing;
whereas Pradhāna, however, undergoes modification through the transformation into another principle?
Thus, since Pradhāna possesses attributes such as being manifold, impure, and insentient, the Puruṣa is its opposite.
That distinction is merely verbal; for if it is argued that the Puruṣa,
who prior to the arising of experience is pure consciousness alone, acquires the so-called "status of an experiencer" at the time experience arises,
and that upon the cessation of experience he returns to being pure consciousness alone, free from that distinction— [we reply that this occurs] through the forms of the Mahat and the other evolutes.

And in this conceptualization—that the *pradhāna* transforms, then departs from it, returns to the *pradhāna*, departs from it again, and finally remains in its own essential nature—there is no distinction whatsoever; thus, a specific modification of the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* is postulated by mere words.
If it is argued that even at the time of experience, the *puruṣa* is nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as it was before, [then the same objection applies].
In that case, enjoyment does not belong to the *puruṣa* from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).

If it is argued that at the time of enjoyment, the modification of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is indeed ultimately real, and therefore enjoyment belongs to the *puruṣa*, we say no; for since the *pradhāna* also possesses modification at the time of enjoyment, it would follow that it too is the enjoyer.

If it is argued that the state of being an enjoyer is merely a modification of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), then there is no logical reason for fire and other elements— which possess unique properties such as heat— not to be enjoyers.
If it is argued that both *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* are enjoyers simultaneously,
this is not so, because it would be impossible for *pradhāna* to exist for the sake of another.

For it is not possible for there to be a relationship of mutual subordinate and principal qualities between the two—the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment—just as it is impossible for two lights to mutually illuminate one another.

If it is argued that the Puruṣa’s state of being an enjoyer consists in the arising of the reflection of consciousness within the mind—which possesses the quality of experience and is composed of *sattva*—despite the Puruṣa being changeless;
we say no, because since there is no distinction in the Puruṣa, the postulation of its being an enjoyer is purposeless.

If suffering in the form of experience does not exist for the *puruṣa* at all times because the *puruṣa* is eternally without distinction, for whose removal would the scripture—the means to liberation—be composed?

If it is argued that the scripture is composed for the purpose of removing sufferings superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*), [we reply: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), the *puruṣa* is only the experiencer and not the agent, while the *pradhāna* is only the agent and not the experiencer; furthermore, there is another ultimately real entity distinct from the *puruṣa*. This conceptualization is outside the scope of scripture and is useless.
And [the view] that it is causeless should not be respected by those seeking liberation.
If it is argued that even if there were unity, the composition of treatises and so forth would be purposeless, we say no; because [in that case] there would be no existence [of duality].
For when there exist authors of treatises and others who seek the fruits thereof, one might entertain the alternative inquiry as to whether the composition of a treatise is purposeless or purposeful.

However, in the case of the oneness of the Self, authors of treatises and so forth do not exist as distinct from that [Self]; thus, in the absence of such agents, the very possibility of such an inquiry is untenable. Furthermore, by you who accept the oneness of the Self, the very purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been accepted. This is because, by accepting the oneness of the Self, you have effectively accepted the utility of a means of knowledge.

And regarding the acceptance of that [state], the scripture states the impossibility of conceptual differentiation: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14), and so forth.
Furthermore, it explains the possibility of the composition of scriptures and the like in a domain other than the nature of the ultimate reality—namely, within the sphere of ignorance:
"For where there is duality, as it were... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
14) Such is the detailed account in the Vājasaneyaka;

and here, in the very beginning of the scripture where knowledge and ignorance, higher and lower, are distinguished, the royal authority of the Vedāntas protects with the strength of its arms this subject of the oneness of the Self. Therefore, no warrior-like opponent of the logicians can enter here.

By this, it should be understood that the objection raised by others—that Brahman lacks the necessary instruments and means for being the agent of creation and so forth, because He possesses a plurality of powers and instruments such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) produced by ignorance (avidyā)—is refuted; as is the objection regarding the Self being the agent of its own misfortune and other such faults. As for the analogy given by them, that the king is called the "agent" through metaphorical attribution to the one who performs all his purposes, that is not applicable here, because it would subvert the primary meaning of the authoritative scripture which states, "He [Brahman] reflected."
For a figurative interpretation of a word occurs only where its primary meaning is impossible.

In this case, however, it is not tenable that the activity of an insentient entity—directed toward a person for the sake of results such as bondage and liberation, and determined with respect to specific persons who are either liberated or bound, as well as with respect to agent, object, place, time, and cause—is possible.

But this is consistent with the position that the omniscient Lord is the creator, as it is by the Lord alone that the vital breath (prāṇa), which presides over all functions, is created by the person.
How did that Person, having looked in the manner described, create the All-breath—known as Hiraṇyagarbha, the self who is the substratum of the organs of all living beings?
From that breath, he created faith, which is the cause of the engagement of all living beings in virtuous action.
Thence, he created the great elements, which serve as the causal foundations and instruments for the experience of the fruits of karma.
Water possesses its own quality of sound, and is characterized by its own quality of touch along with the causal quality [of air], thus possessing three qualities— namely, sound and touch;
likewise, water possesses four qualities through its common quality of taste and the inclusion of the preceding qualities.
Likewise, by the addition of the quality of smell and the inclusion of the preceding qualities, there are four qualities;
likewise, by the addition of the quality of smell and the inclusion of the preceding qualities, the earth possesses five qualities.

Likewise, the sense organ (indriya) initiated by those very same elements is of two kinds—for the purpose of cognition and for the purpose of action—and is tenfold in number; and its presiding lord, situated within, is characterized by doubt and volition.
The mind.
Thus, having created the body (kārya) and the instruments (karaṇa) for living beings, [He created] food characterized by rice, barley, and so forth, for the sake of their maintenance.
And from that food being consumed, vigor—that is, capacity and strength, the means for the engagement in all activities—arises.
And for those living beings possessing vigor, austerity (*tapas*) is the means for achieving purification when they are being corrupted.

From those whose internal and external organs have been purified by austerity, there arise the *mantras*—the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva-Āṅgiras—which serve as the instruments for ritual action (*karman*).
From that [arises] action, characterized by the *agnihotra* and other such rites.
The worlds are the fruit of actions;
and among those [worlds], there are the names of the created living beings, such as Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and so forth.

Thus, these constituent parts (kalās) of living beings are created in dependence upon the seeds of defects such as ignorance (avidyā), just like the vision of two moons, mosquitoes, flies, and so on, produced by one suffering from ophthalmia.
And all objects, like those created by a dreamer, dissolve back into that very same Puruṣa, abandoning the distinctions of name, form, and so forth. //4//

How so? Just as these rivers, flowing along, having the ocean as their goal, reach the ocean and vanish; thus, my dear, the person here who has attained identity with this subtle essence does not know: "I am he"; nor do these creatures know: "This is our father and origin. He becomes that subtle essence, and that subtle essence is the Imperishable (*akṣara*). It is neither gross nor fine, neither short nor long, neither glowing red nor adhesive, neither shadowy nor dark, neither wind nor space; it is without taste, without smell, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without light, without breath, without mouth, without measure, and has no interior or exterior. It consumes nothing whatsoever, and no one consumes it. This is what is called the "Imperishable. Upon attaining this, my dear, the sage becomes free from all desires and freed from all sorrows. It consumes nothing whatsoever, and no one consumes it. This is what is called the 'Imperishable. Upon attaining this, my dear, the sage becomes free from all desires and freed from all sorrows. Thus it is said. "And how, my dear, does he become the very essence of light? "Just as, my dear, when they throw salt into water, it dissolves into the water itself, and from that water one would not be able to take it out; yet, wherever one tastes, it is salty—so indeed, my dear, this great, endless, and limitless Reality is simply Consciousness. Out of this, my dear, the ether is produced; from the ether, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, the sense-faculties; and from the sense-faculties, food. From food comes vital energy, from vital energy faith
Their names and forms are dissolved;
they are simply called "the ocean.
Even so, these sixteen parts of this observer, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and pass away.
And their names and forms are dissolved; he is called simply "the Person. He becomes partless and immortal. Regarding this, there is this verse: PrUp_6.5 //

This is the illustration: just as in the world these rivers flow and stream toward the ocean—the ocean being their *ayana*, their destination, their place of existence—those which have the ocean as their *ayana* reach the ocean, and having reached it, they undergo the disappearance of name and form (*nāmarūpa*).
And for those that have thus disappeared, their names and forms, characterized as "Ganges," "Yamunā," and so forth, are split apart and perish.
When there is no distinction from that [water], the substance characterized as water is called "the ocean";
in this way, according to this illustration, it is so for this Puruṣa under discussion, who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, the all-seeing observer who perceives on all sides.

Just as the sun is the agent of its own self-luminosity, so too these sixteen aforementioned digits (kalās), beginning with prāṇa, have the Puruṣa as their goal—just as the ocean is the goal of rivers. Those digits which have the Puruṣa as their goal reach the Puruṣa; having attained the state of being the Puruṣa, they likewise go to their setting.
The names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) of these *kalās*—designated as "Prāṇa" and so forth—are each distinguished according to their own nature.

And when name and form are divided, that reality which remains undestroyed is declared by the knowers of Brahman to be the *puruṣa*. He who knows this, having been shown by his teacher the path of the dissolution of the *kalās*, [is one for whom] those things born of ignorance, desire, and action have been dissolved away by knowledge.

One who is "without parts" (akala) with respect to the kalās such as prāṇa is indeed immortal upon the disappearance of death, for death has its cause in the kalās produced by ignorance; because he is without parts when that [ignorance] has departed, he becomes immortal.
Regarding this matter, there is this verse: //5//
"As the spokes are fixed in the hub of a wheel, so are all parts established in Him.
Know that Person who is to be known, lest death overwhelm you. (PrUp 6.6)
Just as the spokes are dependent upon the nave of a chariot wheel— meaning they are inserted into the nave of the wheel and rest there—

so too are the *kalās* (the vital breaths and other constituents) established in that Puruṣa during the times of their origin, persistence, and dissolution. One should know— that is, understand— that Puruṣa, who is the very self of the *kalās*, who is to be known because he is all-pervading, or who is called "Puruṣa" because he dwells within the city (*puri śayanāt*).
"O disciples, let not death cause you distress; let it not afflict you.
For if a person were not aware [of this], you would simply fall into the distress caused by death and remain in suffering.
Therefore, the intention is that this [distress] should not be yours. //6//
He said to them:
"I know only this much of that supreme Brahman."
"There is nothing higher than this. (PrU 6.7)

Having thus instructed those disciples, Pippalāda said to them: "I know, indeed, only this much—that which is to be known, the Supreme Brahman. There is nothing higher than this to be known. He spoke thus in order to remove the disciples' suspicion that there might be something remaining unknown, and to produce the realization in them that their purpose had been fulfilled. //7//
They honored him, saying: "You indeed are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore beyond ignorance. Homage!
Homage to the supreme seers! Homage to the supreme seers! (PrUp 6.8)

Then those disciples, having been instructed by their teacher and having achieved their purpose, seeing no further price to pay for their knowledge, what did they do? It is said: honoring and worshipping him at his feet by scattering handfuls of flowers and by prostrating with their heads;
and as to what they said, he says: "For you are our father, because by means of knowledge you have generated for us this eternal, undecaying, immortal, and fearless body of Brahman."

Since you alone, by means of the raft of knowledge, enable us to cross from this shoreless great ocean of ignorance— characterized by the crocodiles of birth, old age, death, disease, suffering, and so forth, arising from our erroneous understanding of our own true nature—
to the further shore known as liberation, which is characterized by supreme non-return; therefore, your status as our father toward us is established, and not that of anyone else.
For even an ordinary father produces only the physical body;
yet he is most worthy of worship in the world—how much more so, then, should one who bestows ultimate fearlessness be praised? This is the intended meaning.
"Salutation to the supreme sages, the founders of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman; salutation to the supreme sages"—the repetition is for the sake of showing reverence. //8//
Thus ends the sixth question. Thus the Praśnopaniṣad is completed.
